args.content:
🌋 Godzilla Docs
  • Concepts
  • Connectors
  • Events
  • Pipelines
  • Schemas

Events

An event is the atomic unit of data that moves through a Pipeline. Every record a source connector emits, every row a transform produces, and every write a destination connector performs is an event.

Event shape

event.json json 
{
  "id": "evt_8f2c1a90",
  "type": "order.created",
  "occurred_at": "2026-08-18T09:12:44Z",
  "source": "connector_postgres_orders",
  "payload": { "order_id": "ord_4471", "amount_cents": 4899 }
}

Every event contains two distinct layers:

  • The envelope — top-level metadata managed by Godzilla (id, type, occurred_at, source).
  • The payload — the domain data object containing your application's fields and records.

Payload schemas and validation

While envelope metadata follows a fixed structure across Godzilla, the contents of the payload are governed by Schemas. Schemas declare the expected fields, data types, and value constraints for each event type.

Godzilla validates incoming event payloads against their schema definition at ingestion and after transform steps. If an event contains an invalid payload (such as missing required properties or wrong type formats), Godzilla enforces the pipeline's validation mode — rejecting the record or routing it to a dead-letter queue before malformed data reaches destination sinks.

For details on declaring payload schemas, validation modes, and schema version evolution, see the Schemas concept guide.

User data events vs. platform events

Godzilla distinguishes two kinds of events:

  • User data events — the records your pipelines process, shaped and validated according to your defined schemas.
  • Platform events — lifecycle notifications Godzilla itself emits: pipeline.started, pipeline.completed, pipeline.failed, connector.error. These are what power Webhooks.
Ordering

Events are delivered in-order per source partition, not globally. Two events from different source partitions may be processed out of order relative to each other.

Retries and dead-lettering

An event that fails a schema validation check (in strict mode), transform, or destination write is retried with exponential backoff. After the configured retry limit, it is moved to that pipeline's dead-letter queue rather than dropped. See Error handling & recovery for how to configure and drain a dead-letter queue.

See also

To query or replay events programmatically, see the Events endpoint in the API reference. For end-to-end recovery workflows and DLQ management, see the Error handling & recovery guide.

Godzilla Docs © Godzilla Docs. All rights reserved.

args.content:
🌋 Godzilla Docs
  • Concepts
  • Connectors
  • Events
  • Pipelines
  • Schemas

Concepts

The core building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.

Start with Pipelines

Godzilla is built from core ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

Concept

Pipelines

Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.

 Concept

Connectors

Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.

 Concept

Events

The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.

 Concept

Schemas

Declarations and validation rules that enforce payload shapes, data types, and compatibility across pipelines.

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, validates their payload against schemas, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that loop.

Definitions

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema
The structural contract and type validation rules for an event's payload moving through a pipeline.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Rate limits.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.
Godzilla Docs © Godzilla Docs. All rights reserved.

🌋 Godzilla Docs
  • API Reference
  • Connectors endpoint
  • Error reference
  • Events endpoint

Rate limits v2 Stable

API rate limits are enforced per workspace using a 60-second sliding window. Limits apply across all pipelines, connectors, and API keys created within the workspace.

100
requests / minute (Developer)

Rate limit for Developer tier API keys per workspace.

1,000
requests / minute (Standard)

Default rate limit for Standard tier API keys per workspace. See Quotas & billing for all plan tiers.

10,000+
requests / minute (Enterprise)

Customizable rate limits for Enterprise plans up to 50,000+ req/min.

Rate limits by plan tier

The table below summarizes the API rate limits and enforcement behavior for each plan tier:

Plan Tier API Rate Limit Window Status Code on Breach
Developer 100 req/min 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests
Standard 1,000 req/min 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests
Enterprise Custom (10,000+) 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests

Rate limit headers

Every response includes X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset. A request over the limit returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

Header Type Description
X-RateLimit-Limit integer The maximum number of requests allowed in the current 60-second sliding window.
X-RateLimit-Remaining integer The number of remaining requests permitted within the current window.
X-RateLimit-Reset integer Unix timestamp (in seconds) indicating when the current sliding rate limit window resets.
Retry-After integer Number of seconds to wait before retrying when a 429 Too Many Requests response is returned.
Need higher limits or hitting quota caps?

If your integration frequently encounters 429 Too Many Requests responses or exceeds monthly event volume, see Quotas & billing to compare plan tiers and understand what happens when quotas are exceeded.

Pagination

List endpoints (Pipelines, Connectors, Events) use cursor-based pagination — a departure from v1's offset-based pagination.

{
  "data": [ { "id": "pl_ingest_orders" } ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjIwfQ",
  "has_more": true
}

Rate limits v2 Stable

API rate limits are enforced per workspace using a 60-second sliding window. Limits apply across all pipelines, connectors, and API keys created within the workspace.

100
requests / minute (Developer)

Rate limit for Developer tier API keys per workspace.

1,000
requests / minute (Standard)

Default rate limit for Standard tier API keys per workspace. See Quotas & billing for all plan tiers.

10,000+
requests / minute (Enterprise)

Customizable rate limits for Enterprise plans up to 50,000+ req/min.

Rate limits by plan tier

The table below summarizes the API rate limits and enforcement behavior for each plan tier:

Plan Tier API Rate Limit Window Status Code on Breach
Developer 100 req/min 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests
Standard 1,000 req/min 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests
Enterprise Custom (10,000+) 60-second sliding window 429 Too Many Requests

Rate limit headers

Every response includes X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, and X-RateLimit-Reset. A request over the limit returns 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.

Header Type Description
X-RateLimit-Limit integer The maximum number of requests allowed in the current 60-second sliding window.
X-RateLimit-Remaining integer The number of remaining requests permitted within the current window.
X-RateLimit-Reset integer Unix timestamp (in seconds) indicating when the current sliding rate limit window resets.
Retry-After integer Number of seconds to wait before retrying when a 429 Too Many Requests response is returned.
Need higher limits or hitting quota caps?

If your integration frequently encounters 429 Too Many Requests responses or exceeds monthly event volume, see Quotas & billing to compare plan tiers and understand what happens when quotas are exceeded.

Pagination

List endpoints (Pipelines, Connectors, Events) use cursor-based pagination — a departure from v1's offset-based pagination.

list-response.json json 
{
  "data": [ { "id": "pl_ingest_orders" } ],
  "next_cursor": "eyJvZmZzZXQiOjIwfQ",
  "has_more": true
}

Webhooks endpoint v2 Stable

Subscribe to platform lifecycle events — such as pipeline.completed or connector.error — as outbound HTTP requests to a URL you control. This is the v2 replacement for v1's polling-only status checks; see the Migration guide if you're moving off v1.

Create a webhook subscription

POST /v2/webhooks

Name Type Required Description
typestringYesHTTPS endpoint Godzilla will POST events to.
eventsarrayYesList of event types to subscribe to, e.g. [\"pipeline.failed\"].
secretstringNoShared secret used to sign the X-Godzilla-Signature header. Auto-generated if omitted.
webhook-payload.json json 
{\n  \"id\": \"evt_wh_2091\",\n  \"type\": \"pipeline.failed\",\n  \"occurred_at\": \"2026-08-18T09:14:02Z\",\n  \"data\": { \"pipeline_id\": \"pl_ingest_orders\", \"error\": \"destination_timeout\" }\n}
Verify the signature

Always verify X-Godzilla-Signature before trusting a webhook payload. Unsigned or unverifiable requests to your endpoint should be rejected, not processed.

Delivery retries

A webhook delivery that doesn't receive a 2xx response is retried with exponential backoff for up to 24 hours, then marked failed. Failed deliveries are visible per-subscription and can be manually redelivered.

Concepts

The core building blocks every Godzilla pipeline is made of.

Start with Pipelines

Godzilla is built from core ideas that compose into everything else in these docs. Understanding how they relate makes the rest of the platform — guides, API reference, SDKs — much easier to follow.

Concept

Pipelines

Named, versioned workflows that move data from a source to a destination through optional transforms.

 Concept

Connectors

Pre-built integrations to external systems — sources, destinations, or both.

 Concept

Events

The atomic unit of data flowing through a pipeline, plus the platform's own lifecycle events.

 Concept

Schemas

Declarations and validation rules that enforce payload shapes, data types, and compatibility across pipelines.

How they fit together

A pipeline reads events from a source connector, validates their payload against schemas, transforms them, and writes them to a destination connector. Everything else in Godzilla — retries, webhooks, monitoring — is built on top of that loop.

Definitions

Short definitions for every term used throughout these docs.

Pipeline
A named, versioned workflow that moves data from a source connector, through optional transforms, to a destination connector.
Connector
A pre-built integration to an external system — a source, a destination, or both.
Event
The atomic unit of data moving through a pipeline, or a platform lifecycle notification like pipeline.failed.
Schema
The structural contract and type validation rules for an event's payload moving through a pipeline.
Webhook
An outbound HTTP request Godzilla sends to a URL you control when a subscribed event occurs.
Dead-letter queue
Where an event goes after exhausting its retries, rather than being dropped. See Error handling & recovery.
Cursor pagination
The pagination style used by every v2 list endpoint. See Rate limits.
Workspace
The top-level account boundary an API key is scoped to.
